parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what type of particle leaves a metal and where it was before it left.
Hint 2: Think about what must arrive at the metal surface to cause that release.
parts.proper_answer: The emission of electrons from a metal surface when electromagnetic radiation is incident on the surface.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the metal surface**
Imagine light shining onto a clean metal plate in a vacuum. Inside the metal there are free electrons, but normally they do not have enough energy to escape. You are being asked for the name of the process where they do escape.

Step 2: **Add the cause and the effect**
The cause is incident electromagnetic radiation, which arrives as photons. The effect is that an electron absorbs the photon energy and, if that energy is large enough, it is emitted from the surface. So the full definition needs both halves: emission of electrons (from metal) + when e.m. radiation is incident.

parts.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: photoelectric equation hf = work function + max kinetic energy
hints: Hint 1: Think about what $V_S$ physically does to the emitted electrons - why would even the fastest electrons fail to reach the other plate?
Hint 2: Think about what controls how much kinetic energy those fastest electrons start with, using the idea of one photon giving energy to one electron.
Hint 3: Link the energy of a single photon to the frequency $f$ of the light.
parts.proper_answer: Current falls to zero when $eV_S$ equals the maximum initial kinetic energy of the photoelectrons. Photon energy is $hf$ so depends on $f$, and $E_{max} = hf - \Phi$ so depends on photon energy. Hence $V_S$ depends on $f$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What $V_S$ really measures**
In Fig. 9.1 the potentiometer makes plate X negative relative to emitting plate Y, so it repels the electrons. As $V$ is increased fewer electrons can climb the potential hill to X. At $V = V_S$ even the most energetic electrons are just stopped, so:
$$eV_S = E_{max}$$
where $E_{max}$ is the maximum kinetic energy at emission. That is why $V_S$ is called the stopping potential.

Step 2: **Bring in photons**
Light arrives as photons, each with energy:
$$E_{photon} = hf$$
One photon is absorbed by one electron. Part of the energy is needed to escape the metal (the work function $\Phi$), the rest becomes kinetic energy:
$$hf = \Phi + E_{max}$$
So $E_{max}$ depends directly on the photon energy.

Step 3: **Join the chain**
Because $E_{photon}$ depends on $f$, then $E_{max}$ depends on $f$, and because $V_S = E_{max}/e$, then $V_S$ must depend on $f$. Higher $f$ gives more energetic photons, faster electrons, and a larger stopping voltage is needed to stop them.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: work function and Planck constant from gradient
hints: Hint 1: Look first at Fig. 9.3 where the line meets the $f$-axis - what does $V_S = 0$ tell you about the minimum frequency for emission?
Hint 2: Look at the straight-line part of Fig. 9.3 - recall that $V_S = (h/e)f - \Phi/e$, so what do gradient and intercept give you?
Hint 3: Look at Fig. 9.2 at $V = 0$ where the current is largest - how can you turn that saturation current into a number of electrons, and hence photons, per second?
parts.proper_answer: e.g. threshold frequency $f_0 = 1.5 \times 10^{15}\text{ Hz}$; work function $\Phi = hf_0 = 9.9 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J} = 6.2\text{ eV}$; Planck constant $h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$ from gradient of $V_S$ against $f$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read threshold frequency from Fig. 9.3**
$V_S = 0$ means $E_{max} = 0$, the just-emitted case. From the graph the line starts at:
$$f_0 = 1.5 \times 10^{15}\text{ Hz}$$
Below this no electrons are emitted however intense the light. The corresponding threshold wavelength is:
$$\lambda_0 = c/f_0 \approx 2.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}$$

Step 2: **Use gradient to find $h$ and work function**
From $eV_S = hf - \Phi$:
$$V_S = \frac{h}{e}f - \frac{\Phi}{e}$$
So gradient $= h/e$. From Fig. 9.3, e.g. rise $\approx 6.2\text{ V}$ for run $3.0-1.5 = 1.5 \times 10^{15}\text{ Hz}$:
$$\frac{h}{e} \approx 4.1 \times 10^{-15}\text{ V s}$$
$$h \approx 4.1 \times 10^{-15} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \approx 6.6 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$$
The work function follows from $hf_0$:
$$\Phi = hf_0 \approx 9.9 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J} \approx 6.2\text{ eV}$$

Step 3: **Use Fig. 9.2 saturation current for photon rate**
At $V = 0$ in stage 1 ($f = 2.5 \times 10^{15}\text{ Hz}$) the current is about $2.7\text{ mA}$. This is all photoelectrons collected, so with $I = Ne$:
$$N = I/e \approx \frac{2.7 \times 10^{-3}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 1.7 \times 10^{16}\text{ s}^{-1}$$
Assuming one photon releases one electron, this is also the photon arrival rate. Incident power is then:
$$P = Nhf \approx 1.7 \times 10^{16} \times 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 2.5 \times 10^{15} \approx 0.028\text{ W}$$
Any three of these quantitative values earns credit.
